newsitem.title: BELGIUM: French time-change plan counted out by EU.
newsitem.headline: French time-change plan counted out by EU.

text.p: France lost on Tuesday its campaign to abandon a twice-yearly change to its clocks when EU transport ministers rejected Paris's arguments for ditching European rules to synchronise the change.

"We were beaten," French Secretary of State for Transport Anne-Marie Idrac told reporters. "Europe is something which is built by more than one country. Today, we must conclude that our arguments weren't followed."

The ministers' decision, which must be cleared by the European Parliament before final adoption, means that for the four years from 1998, EU countries will sunchronise their clock changes in March and October.
Idrac said that for 1997 and 1998 France would march in step with the rest of the EU while for the two following years she said only: "We'll see."

European Union countries, in common with many non-equatorial states around the world, advance their clocks one hour in the Spring and put them back again in the Autumn so as to provide an extra hour of daylight in the evening.
Southern EU countries like Greece, Italy, Spain and Portugal have argued that longer evenings boost their busy tourist trades, allowing museums and other services to stay open longer.

France wanted to keep the same time all year round, a position backed by the country's powerful farming lobby, which said the change disrupted farm work such as milking cows, and some parents, who said it upset babies and school children.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe also dislikes the daylight-saving measure, originally introduced in the 1970s to save energy but now an increasingly politicised issue in France.

French arguments won scant support from other EU countries on Tuesday, bar a sympathetic ear from Britain which said that changing clocks was a sovereign right not an EU matter, a spokesman for European Transport Commissioner Neil Kinnock said.
France did secure the promise of yet another study of the merits and disadvantages of the practice, this one by the European Commission, to be delivered to ministers no later than June 30, 1999.
The spokesman said the Commissioner accepted the task.
"Kinnock has no problem with that although he recalled that there have already been two reports on this," he said.
Failure to agree new rules would have left a legal limbo for 1998, creating confusion for timetable planners in schools and scheduled transport businesses.
